God decides to create a nation that will be an exemplary model for others, naming it Israel. He identifies Abraham as the patriarch of this nation, who is also recognized in Christianity and Islam as their ancestor. Thus, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam are collectively referred to as Abrahamic faiths.

Yahweh forms a covenant with Abraham, requiring loyalty and exclusive worship from his followers. Abraham questions Yahweh’s decision to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah due to their wickedness. Instead of submitting, he engages in a debate with Yahweh, arguing for the preservation of even a small number of righteous individuals within the cities.

Yahweh initially agrees to spare the cities if 50 righteous people are found but is willing to reduce this number down to just 10. This interaction illustrates that the relationship between Abraham and Yahweh is more akin to a friendship, with both parties openly debating moral and ethical issues. This dynamic underpins the power of Judaism as it fosters debate and questioning.

Abraham’s son Isaac is born, leading to the lineage of Jacob, who later renames himself Israel. Through cunning, Jacob takes his older brother Esso's birthright from their father Isaac with the help of his mother Rebecca.
